The minister's wish was for us to be there because given the task and the seriousness thereof, we were supposed to practically represent him down there and to provide overall support to the police units deployed down there and also to have certain liaison with the socio-political structures in Pristina and on the ground. Both General Stevanovic and I were specifically tasked with being on the ground wherever the operations were in progress in order to encourage members of the Ministry of the Interior who were carrying out the tasks and maybe dying in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, did the minister orally change the powers and jurisdiction of the staff that had been set up?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't change anything. Sreten Lukic remained in his position on the head of the staff with the same composition, only he was obligated to brief him about everything on a daily basis and to be on the premises of the staff constantly, to be in permanent touch with the minister so that the minister would be informed or maybe to receive some feedback information or orders from the minister concerning our activities. Our primary task given by him was to be with the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You already told us that. Can you tell us in concrete terms, what happened in the aftermath of that meeting with the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the 21st of July. In the early evening of that day or maybe early morning of the next day, we went to Pristina, and we continued to perform what the minister had entrusted us with doing. I have to say as regards all these relationships because I didn't mention that on two or one occasion I was at the head of this staff and the last time it happened was in 1998, I was at the head of this staff in Pristina. When I left -- I'm talking about certain relationships with the army and other structures - my principal obligation when I went down there to stand-in for the head of the then-head of staff, my first obligation was during the take over of duties to visit the command of the Pristina Corps, to get myself acquainted with the commander of the Pristina Corps, and in that way establish certain rapport with him that would in the future probably be necessary in some joint actions with the Yugoslav Army. My next task as well as the task of all other heads of the staff was to familiarise myself with the political structures existing in Kosovo at the time. What I can say is that in view of the prevailing political situation and the leaving of certain officials from the political structures, the Government of Serbia from 1990 had its own representative in Kosovo and Metohija who was answerable to the Government of the Republic of Serbia for the situation there. I know that because together with him, when I was at the head of the staff, I went to Kosovo and I know that at the time Dusan Mihajlovic was representing the Government of Serbia in Kosovo, who was at the time a coalition partner of Slobodan Milosevic and his party, and he was vice prime minister of the Government of Serbia. The two of us went down there together. His obligation, as I mentioned, was to monitor the overall situation and co-ordinate with other state organs in Pristina and throughout the territory on behalf of the Serbian government. After he finished his mission there, according to the plan, ministers would go down there and they would do the same job as the vice prime minister. If there was some extraordinary situation, then the government would appoint a minister to be down there, but at all times there was representatives of the government of the -- Serbia in Kosovo. Zoran Andjelkovic was the last representative and at the same time, he was the chairman of the provisional Executive Council. Our obligation was to establish contact with the representatives of the Government of Serbia and the Yugoslav Army, and our obligation was also to occasionally report to all the structures about what was going on because these representatives of the Government of Serbia had to be updated at all times about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and with the obligations that we as the ministry had. This is how we acted after this meeting as well and after the minister had designated myself and General Obrad Stevanovic to stay in the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell me, what year was it that you were in Kosovo -- no, that you were the head of this staff last. It is for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1990 or 1991. I was -- we had rotating heads every six months. Later it was a year's term, but the tasks and the terms of reference were equal in respect of the structures in the province and in the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just told us that representatives of political structures were there, were always present down there. Tell me, at the time when you arrived there in July 1998 who was there, from what political echelons?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting as well we were informed by President Milosevic that representatives of the political establishment and of the state of both the Republic of Serbia and of Yugoslavia would also be there in Kosovo. These were people that we knew, and it was on that basis that we later continued to mutually exchange information, to meet, in order first of all to generally implement this plan; and secondly, to meet the specific needs of the people in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me the names of the persons that you co-operated with in July 1998, also in the implementation of that plan.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was the provisional leader of the provisional Executive Council of Kosovo, that was Zoran Andjelkovic; Milomir Minic was also there who at the time held a high office in the Federal Assembly; then the vice premier, Nikola Sainovic, was there; and a businessman was also there, he was the director of Sartid, and I believe for a while he was a minister of one of the governments, and the cabinets changed quite frequently at that time; Dusan Matkovic was also there, and that was the political echelon or people who were, according to their respective lines of work, charged with monitoring the situation and acting accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: During the period of the implementation of this plan, did other people, other politicians, come to Kosovo and Metohija with a view to rehabilitating the political situation and improving the situation in Kosovo generally?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very often other representatives from other structures would arrive. If the need arose in the assessment of the cabinet, also other ministers would be assigned to go down there. The chief of the state security department, Jovica Stanisic, would come; the assistant minister, Radomir Markovic, also occasionally arrived in Kosovo; and if the assessment was -- the minister's assessment was that there should be other people visiting the area, they did so at his instructions, doing their duties as we discharge our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the minister himself come?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the minister also visited, and he had meetings with us who were down there, and we, as his assistants, namely, General Stevanovic and I myself, also had a duty to occasionally go to Belgrade to report to him, to brief him on the situation, and he had already established his relationship with General Lukic in the envisaged way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, I can see from your previous statement that the police had already conducted certain activities, not just certain activities, but had definite activities in Kosovo and Metohija prior to the commencement of the implementation of this plan. What was the situation concerning the police units like before the plan started to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the plan started to be implemented, the units discharged certain duties which I have already indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just not to belabour the point, please just tell me the number of units and whether they were already present there then, and we shall later discuss the actual activities.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1990 and in fact from 1989, practically from the time of the setting up of all the staffs that were there in this period, practically from 1980 there were always police forces from outside, from the other republics, and when only the Republic of Serbia remained from the Republic of Serbia, there were always policemen attached to the secretariats of the police down there, to assist them, because personnel-wise they were not adequately equipped and capable to deal with the situation because the ethnic Albanians had left the service. So in terms of their numbers the secretariats were undermanned, and they always needed a number of policemen to be engaged from other quarters. The number of policemen who were sent to help out the secretariats depended on the prevailing security situation in Kosovo generally speaking and in terms of the respective secretariats. So sometimes more people would be sent to the secretariat where the situation was more demanding, but there was always a number of policemen from Serbia in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told me that you went to Pristina after this meeting with the minister. Were the units already ready to implement this plan at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the units were already down there, and the rest during the time when we had this meeting with the minister -- actually, at that time the minister instructed that we were to engage all the PJPs. And in accordance with that, the police administration, following his orders, took measures to dispatch the necessary number of units for engagement of specific tasks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Exhibit P768.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is number 84 for you, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Djordjevic, we see on our screen minutes from the meeting of the MUP staff of the 22nd of July, 1998. And I can see your name also featuring in the heading. Do you recall this meeting; and if you do, can you tell us what was the subject and how the meeting unfolded.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this meeting with the minister, he instructed us that on the next day when we were to go down there the head of the staff was to call a meeting with the heads of the secretariat and with the staff, and that we as his assistants were also to attend that meeting. According to these minutes, and I know that the -- this is generally the case, the heads of the secretariats briefly reported on the situations in their respective areas. And then we briefed them, we who had been at that meeting with the minister, we briefed them on their future obligations, the obligations of the staff, or the obligations that they would have to discharge in future activities against the terrorists. We acquainted them with the fact that the general plan had been adopted, that the Yugoslav Army and the police would participate in its implementation, that we would be working together, that we would be discharging very difficult and responsible tasks, and that that is why we were there, to see to it that those tasks would indeed be successfully completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, we heard some witnesses here refer to the fact that at this meeting on the 22nd of July there was word or so of the existence of a Joint Command. Would you be so kind as to tell us whether you heard at all about the term or knew at all about the concept of a Joint Command at the time this meeting was held, which you also attended?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment we neither considered such a term nor did it exist at all nor was it customary when police activities are concerned for any Joint Command to exist or to be set up. We normally work with staffs. This is the way -- this is the philosophy of police work, this is our perception. What we did say was that we would be working together with the army, that we would be jointly undertaking activities, and that it was a state priority, so that all structures would have to be involved to the full in that and to work synchronously. That is what we told the heads of the secretariats so that at that particular time this term, "Joint Command," meant nothing nor was there any reason to use it. We did say that we would be working together with the army, but no one referred to nor used the term "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But when was it that you first heard of the use of this term, "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was later, when we had these co-ordination meetings to exchange information, when we participated at meetings together with the army, this is the term they used because this is something which is in normal use in the army. So perhaps just by way of some inertia we also used the word Joint Command, but this is a military term. It was used by the army. This is a term which is alien to us. We were not members of any Joint Command nor did we function as a Joint Command. This was a term that was used by the army and they know how they used it and why they used it. It is a term which is -- which belongs to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us a while ago that at this meeting with the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia no commander of the forces to implement this global plan was appointed, was named. Tell me now, when you arrived in Pristina, how was -- how were things organised, how was control and command of the units organised, all the participating units organised in order to realise the global plan?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, at that meeting with President Milosevic -- at President Milosevic's, we were charged with a specific task. We knew who was to prepare the plans. The minister instructed us as there was no other option, no other solution, but for us to liaise with the leadership of the Pristina Corps who were to make the specific segments of this global plan. So the minister ordered us, as was the case also generally and in previous cases, for us to get in touch down there with the military structures and to agree with them about how we shall go about realising this global plan. And this was the only way for us to proceed. But even before this meeting that we had with the heads of the SUPs, we had already talked to the commander of the Pristina Corps, and we agreed to -- we made a date for that evening to see -- to have a meeting that evening to agree about our further course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this meeting that evening indeed held; and if so, who attended it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held on the 22nd of July, and it was attended also by the political representatives who had attended the meeting at Milosevic's office. From the police was the head of the staff, his deputy, namely, General Obrad Stevanovic and I myself; and from the Pristina Corps it was the corps commander who attended the meeting and Colonel Djakovic, whom I believe I saw for the first time at that time and who from then on continued to be with us; and these politicians that I referred to previously were also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was on the agenda of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topic discussed at the meeting was that we were to commence the implementation of this global plan. In order for this general plan to be realised, we had to -- it had to evolve in stages. There were individual documents prepared for every singular anti-terrorist activity. Then General Pavkovic, as he was the sole person who had a plan and nobody else did, he informed us what our tasks would be in this first stage. The obligation stemming from this operationally speaking first stage were to deblock, unblock, these roads. And then he told us that in accordance with the plan the first road to be lifted the blockade from was the Pristina-Pec road from two directions as well as other roads. That evening the ministry staff was also charged with identifying its obligations and designating the units that would be used to lift the blockade off the roads. Following that meeting and agreement, the next day obligations at staff level as well as at corps level were discussed, and after the staff had decided what units would be used on what axes, one of the representatives of the staff went to the Pristina Corps with -- and submitted -- practically submitted data on that to General Djakovic so that General Djakovic could draw up a specific order and the relevant document which he is normally to draw up in keeping with military regulations. So the representative of the MUP staff actually provided the terms of reference in the -- in terms of which units would be engaged, and this was technically actually put together and translated into a concrete plan by the general from the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us how the general plan would be elaborated in the specific segments. Tell me, after it had been technically drawn up, what was the further procedure that was followed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in order to be generally able to act and it was necessary to urgently act, or rather, as soon as possible, this had to be done first. So after Pavkovic's briefing and hearing the obligations that each of us were assigned with to that effect, notably the staff, we took these measures. On the following day, as soon as the technical elaboration of the plan had been completed, on the premises of the staff -- or rather, in the building of the then-provincial secretariat where the staff was headquartered, we organised a meeting with all commanders of military units of the military units which were envisaged to participate in the implementation of this first stage and the commanders of all the police units that were also to be engaged. This meeting was attended by all of us, that means us from the corps command, the head of the MUP staff, General Obrad, and I myself. At that meeting documents were prepared, they were given to the commanders of military units and to the commanders of the PJPs, the special police units. These documents were handed out to them as well as the particular segments from the document elaborated by Colonel Djakovic, and upon receiving all these documents, the commanders that were to act in concert in the operations as envisaged by the plan were actually familiarised with their respective assignments and thereby the meeting ended. And then the commanders returned to their respective areas to commence the preparations for the respective parts of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go step by step, please. First of all, what particular segments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the time, Mr. Djurdjic. You seem to be going down quite a long road. We will interrupt, I think, and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, this representative of the staff who went to the Pristina Corps command, who gave him his tasks to convey to them concerning the engagement of police units in those operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the head of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever issue such tasks?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When that individual plan was ready -- you said the Pristina Corps made sections of the plan. Where were the plans sent?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained what happened with the first plans and the preparation of documents for the first stage of the implementation. We gathered all police and army commanders in one place, the military commander received an envelope with his section, and the police commander with his own. The police -- for the police commands and units, that plan was final. According to the section of the plan as prepared, the Pristina Corps commander went to the ground and executed his own. The first time these plans were handed to them directly because we wanted them to be gathered in one place and to meet one another because they were about to engage in a giant activity, but in future operations, in those that followed, the plans were made in the same way but they were not handed -- the sections were not handed the same way. A representative of the corps would pick up their section of the plan and then he would familiarise individual units with the tasks concerning them, and a representative of the staff took the police section of the plan. From what I could see on the ground, I saw only a coded map of the area where the unit was active, and that coded map contained a numeric designation of a place, let's say a village. The MUP staff had a plan, had a map like that, the co-ordinating unit as well, and the Pristina Corps as well. So when a commander calls in from the ground and says, "I'm close to the village 33," the staff can look at the map, see number 33, and then they know where the unit is. And in co-ordination with that unit, they can call up the commander and say, "I am moving in from direction such and such," so the military commander also knows where the police unit is. The same would happen in the relations between the corps and the centre, and that's the only thing I saw on the ground. I don't know if the MUP staff had maybe a plan of communications in addition to the map, a list of code-names so that they know which commander, which unit, is using which code in radio communications. Everyone had a call-sign, but the plan for police units would be the section of the plan made at the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of these units on the ground, police and army units?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ground everyone commanded their own unit, thus the commander of the combat group or a military unit would be their regular commander. The commander of the police was the commander of the PJP or the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit or the unit for special operations controlled by the state security; in other words, everyone acted according to their own plan under the documents sent from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which units were involved in the implementation of this overall plan in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: PJP units, the Special Anti-Terrorist Units from the public security sector, and the unit for special operation, JSO, from the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: After all these activities to execute individual plans, to whom did police unit commander report, if they reported, and how?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any moment in time, commanders kept in touch and informed the staff about the course of the operation, and if they needed any additional assistance to successfully complete their mission. And after completion they would also report to the staff, but I don't know whether they would actually go there to report verbally or write a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And did you receive reports from these commanders after completion of activities?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, nor were they required to report to me after finishing an operation. If I was on the ground already with the commanders, they would tell me about the operation, but after an operation was completed nobody would report to me because reporting was done to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us specifically now what you did when you went to Kosovo on the 21st and 22nd of July while this programme was being implemented?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, in the first few days before these operations began in end July - I've already described my activities - and after that, following the minister's orders, I went to the areas where the most difficult situation was expected. I toured the secretariats there and contacted other agencies at the level of the secretariat, and when I was on the axis where operations were conducted, I was in touch with the commanders, and they would tell me if they needed assistance from any other agencies. If I was able to, I provided that assistance. If there were any issues on the ground that required something to be done to facilitate that work, I would try to do something about that. Civilians there needed to be protected, therefore I contacted with both the secretariats in those areas and the units in charge of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when you be in the field with a SUP or with a unit performing an operation, did you issue any orders?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not issue any orders. I was not able to change the orders that had been issued and backed up with documents. I was sometimes able to lend assistance in other matters, but to act as a commander in a particular situation, in a particular area, that I could not do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The commanders of police and military units acting in one and the same area, how would they co-operate?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having received the sections of the plans that I've referred to, every commander of one force would know with which commander of the other force to co-ordinate. Before an operation they would meet and look at the map together to identify each other's actions, and they would agree on how to start the execution. In the course of execution, they would be together or very close to one another most of the time, so they had direct contact. And if direct contact was impossible, then they would communicate by radio. Therefore, before operations police and army commanders would be in touch because their units were executing the same task. And for this to be successful, they had to be well informed minute by minute of the situation on the ground and the location of their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were police unit commanders able to issue orders to army unit commanders or vice versa, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was first and foremost co-operation and interaction between units that were commanded each by its own commander. The army knew what its job was and the police also. Nobody exchanged commanders. The commanders would meet before an operation to agree on everything, but no police commander could issue orders to the army, nor could an army commander issue orders to the police. They could only ask for assistance from one another. For instance, military units could be asked to put more weight on one axis than another or an army commander could ask a police commander to send him a company, or a squad, or a platoon. But that was a system of co-operation and co-ordination, not through the system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the MUP staff for fighting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija issued orders to the Pristina Corps or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP staff was never able to issue an order to military units. That is precisely why co-operation with the corps command was necessary. Everything that had to be taken care of at that level, the MUP staff would settle with the corps command, and the corps command would issue orders accordingly to its units. In the same way, the Pristina Corps, if it had any requests, could address the staff, discuss with them, and everyone was able to assist or meet the other's requests within a system of co-operation. But nothing happened because one force issued orders to another. Our task was to achieve maximum co-operation in each operation, and it was in that spirit that tasks were issued and implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As assistant minister and chief of the public security sector who was present at the implementation of this global plan, did you issue any orders to the MUP staff for fighting terrorism? Did you participate in the planning, organisation, and controlling of police units in those co-ordinated actions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not able to issue them with any instructions or tasks. They had already received them from the minister. That is one. And two, the MUP staff had experts, qualified people who were perfectly able to plan, decide how each mission would be executed, and what needed to be asked from the Pristina Corps in terms of assistance in order to successfully carry out the police tasks. Orders and related activities and control over police units was executed exclusively through the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, you were in Pristina for a long time after the beginning of the implementation of the global plan. Where was your base?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an office in the same building which housed the staff. I would go back there after an operation or before an operation to use the telephone to call the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have any feedback on the activities of the units and the developments in the area of Kosovo and Metohija related to the plan?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about reporting to the minister on the situation, the progress of actions and security-related events, how did that go during the implementation of the plan?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the staff would inform the minister daily on all the activities, planned activities as well, and upon completion of an activity they would also discuss other issues that the head of the staff thought necessary to discuss with the minister. So the head of the staff informed the minister daily, and the minister, if he had any other instructions to give, that was an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you also in contact with the minister while you were down there staying in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, not that frequently, not every day. There was no need for that, but I occasionally called him. He asked for me to call him occasionally and mainly we maintained contact, and he was informed about what I was doing, what the situation was like from my angle of perception, and that is how I was in touch with the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you on occasion go to Belgrade as well?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Over the three months that I spent down there, I went to Belgrade several times, stayed there a couple of days, depending on the obligations that I had to discharge, either within the ministry or elsewhere. After that I would return down there. There was a lot of mail which needed signing, so I would take advantage of those couple of days to do so, and occasionally my chef de cabinet brought all the mail to me to Pristina to sign because there was a huge back-log, so I would sign them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, you were the assistant minister and chief of the department. How did your department function while you were in Pristina during the implementation of this global plan?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work unfolded in this way: Practically the role of the chief of the department was assumed at that time by the minister. As we said previously, he had weekly collegium meetings at which he issued assignments to the services. He directly liaised with his assistants who were in Belgrade. He also maintained direct contact with the chiefs of administrations who were in Belgrade, so that in principle he was kept abreast of the overall situation in the public security department, and he accordingly issued the necessary instructions to the services which they carried out into practice -- carried out in practice. As far as I was concerned, I could talk on the telephone, get in touch with some of the different lines of work heads, and I could be briefed on what was happening there; and therefore, I was informed. I did not have whilst in Kosovo contact with the heads of the SUPs, which I normally liaised with whilst in Belgrade, so that according to the minister's order my primary duty at that time, in that period, was the situation in Kosovo monitoring the overall situation in Kosovo and the implementation of the global counter-terrorism plan. So as far as my regular duties in Belgrade are concerned, I sort of left that aside, shall I say, but as soon as I returned to Belgrade I assumed my regular duties as chief of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As this realisation of the plan actually lasted over a lengthy period, tell me how were the units replaced, rotated, replenishments, supplies of equipment and armaments, how was that done? Who sent the requests? How were they accommodated during the realisation of the plan?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the staff of the Ministry of the Interior in Pristina there was a man from the police administration, precisely from the department dealing with special police units and the reserve force, who monitored the overall situation regarding the forces necessary for the staff and regarding the replacement of the existing forces by new forces or the additional engagement of forces. Thus, in keeping with the assessed required number of police members and police units in the staff, this -- the head of the staff or his assistant who was seized of these matters would address the police administration with a request for replacements or replenishments, or the dispatching of a new unit. Pursuant to such a request, the police administration - and in keeping with the general instructions from the minister for all units to be used down in Kosovo - would prepare dispatches, issue orders to the Secretariats of the Interior, for them to undertake the necessary preparations and to dispatch to the staff in Kosovo or to the secretariats down there in Kosovo, and entire unit, a part of the unit, or the necessary number of policemen. So the technical aspect of the dispatching of units was dealt with along the lines of the staff, the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were staying in Pristina, did you attend meetings of the staff, of the staff, the core meetings and the extended meetings, c-o-r-e meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was able sometimes to attend meetings of the staff when I assessed that there was some important topic that I needed to be there for, I would attend the meeting; but the staff was constantly in operation and constantly in session and constantly monitoring the situation, and I did not attend all its meetings but just occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please repeat when you said -- when I asked you about attendance at meetings in the staff. What was your presence there like for the sake of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I occasionally attended meetings of the staff. It was not my obligation to attend them, but when so necessary or when I assessed that I should be there I was there. I attended those meetings, and I took part in the work of the meetings, contributing to them with some proposals of mine or helping them in any way I thought I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be so kind as to speak slowly for the sake of the interpreter and the transcript so that we don't waste any time. Mr. Djordjevic, in the conducting of these anti-terrorist actions, what was the behaviour of the units vis-à-vis the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that special attention was being devoted to that particular issue, namely, when anti-terrorist activities were being carried out, care was taken to avoid the civilian population coming to any harm. And to the best of my knowledge, in 1998 this was successfully managed to do. There might have been some minor incidents, but generally speaking the treatment of the civilians at the hands of the police and the army was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard some witnesses here who talked about the use of force by the police. Tell us, in what way did the police use force, and was it directed at civilians, or was it not directed at them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our primary task was to clear the blockade of the roads. This lifting of the blockade was carried out by neutralising all the fortifications that had been installed, and the activities of the police were directed primarily at such roads. As regards to settlements that were along those roads, part of those villages were also encircled by some fortifications from which resistance was offered and from which the police were attacked and which had to be neutralised. In that sense the police units -- and the police units acted in that sense. Later when we encountered the major strongholds with most inveterate terrorists where they were best organised, at entrances to these villages where they were, they would be fortified along the axis of the expected arrival of the police. They fortified their positions as often as not, including the first houses in the villages, and there were as a rule deep trenches in front of all those houses. And from that, from such positions, they offered resistance to the police forces as they arrived or they attacked the police forces as they were arriving. In order to crush such resistance the police had to use adequate assets to neutralise such fortifications. However, when afterwards the police entered such villages, it would establish that in fact there had been no civilians at all in those villages and that practically prior to the arrival of the police or military units along the expected axis of their movement, according to orders issued by someone civilians had left those villages and then the terrorists could use those areas from which to offer resistance to the police. After entering the area, having crushed the resistance and destroyed the erected barricades from where the terrorists were withdrawing, as they withdrew they as a rule ended up with the civilians who had been relocated previously, and it was in remote forest areas or other villages. There they would reunite with the civilians, merge with them, discard their arms, and afterwards the police units would encounter such civilians and take adequate action in their regards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But tell me, were these actions that you undertook at targeting the civilians from villages?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police had available information what villages were the known strongholds, what villages were the ones most often used by the terrorists, and the police had the intention to and focused its activities only on terrorists, never on civilians, because there was no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in these places where actions were undertaken, did the KLA offer any resistance? Was there any fighting between the forces, the security forces of the FRY and Serbia and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Virtually every village had its security guards and its fortifications so that the -- there was fighting practically along all axes where the police was focusing in its activities. There was always fighting, but the fighting was always with terrorists and not civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who decided which level of force, which kind of weapons, in other words, were to be used in the fighting that went on?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were decisions taken by commanders on the ground, namely, the principal of the Yugoslav Army in compliance with the obligations stemming for it from the global plan and in agreement with the Pristina Corps had the obligation to support the forces of the ministry and to use the assets available to it to destroy fortifications, strongholds, and barricades that the police was unable to destroy with its own resources. After having destroyed them in this way or after having used its resources in this way -- after the army having used its resources in this way, then the police stepped in to take those area and to inspect them and see whether there still were any terrorists there or not. The actual intensity, the level of the use of resources, depended on the actual strength of the fortifications that the units encountered, which also determined the actual resources to be used to neutralise such strongholds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were on the ground, can you tell us, can you describe for us, a village household, a village estate, a village household of the Albanians of the Muslim faith there.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've heard time and again from Albanian witnesses themselves what their households looked like, but a village or a village household in principle, in principle are encircled by high stone or concrete or concrete block walls. They are enclosed from the street side and from the sides laterally, and they are very amenable to resistance being offered from them, being offered such good protection by these walls from any police or army forces. So these facilities were favourable for such resistance and they were indeed used for such resistance to be offered to army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that our time for today is running out or has expired in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now then, Mr. Djurdjic, to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 4th day of December, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
